Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Justice) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 27, to amend the Juvenile Delinquents Act, 1908.
He said: The object of this bill is to give additional jurisdiction to the Juvenile Court, increase the amount of fines and modify the rules of procedure, this being recommended and asked for by various judges of the Juvenile Court and by other bodies.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

Mr. E. R. E. CHEVRIER (Ottawa) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 28 to amend and make operative certain provisions of the Copyright Act, 1921.
He said:	This bill contains a considerable
number of amendments to the Copyright Act, which was passed by the House last session. In view of the manner in which bills are now being printed, I think at this stage it will not be necessary for me to make any lengthy statement as the reasons for these amendments all appear on the notes opposite to the sections to which they refer. Briefly, this bill is introduced for the purpose, amongst other things, of defining certain very important terms that are used in the Copyright Act which are not defined at present. It is also introduced for the purpose of repealing what are known as the license clauses, 13, 14, IS and 27 of the present act, and which in the minds of the authors or the publishers constitute one of the most arbitrary discriminations against authors. The bill has also for its object the extending and making more operative certain sections of the act which refer to the protection which was intended to be given to the authors, but which is not extended because of the present state of the law. The fourth feature of the bill is to remove this matter from the jurisdiction of the Department of Trade and Commerce and place it under the jurisdiction of the Department of Justice.
I may say this bill in no way affects any of the rights of the printers or those who are engaged in similar industries, but is simply for the purpose of extending the protection which the authors claim in the first place they were entitled to by virtue of this act.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

I was not aware that this resolution would be debated to-day. I have listened with a good deal of interest to some of the statements which have been made, and particularly to the references that have been made to a resolution calling for the transferable or alternative vote which was passed at the last session of parliament. A good many things have happened during the past year; a good deal of light has been thrown on the actions and motives of some of the people of this Dominion as well as of other countries, and I think it is about time that we were speaking frankly what we believe to be the fact, and that we should cast aside this camouflage which has been attempted by a good many people of this Dominion so far as political parties are concerned.
To my mind the object that is sought by the alternative vote, which is coupled with this resolution, is one that is intended to *arry out the designs of the members of the .wo parties calling themselves the Progressive party and the Liberal party, whereas, as a matter of fact, there is absolutely no difference between the two. I think the people of this country thoroughly understand their object, what they have in view, and the means by which they are going to take advantage in a scheme of this kind. For that reason I must say that I am absolutely opposed to any further experiments along the line suggested by the most impractical members of the House, the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Good), and his colleague the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster). 6. Routing and interchange of traffic.
The Canadian Northern and the constituent and subsidiary companies severally agree with the government as follows:	[DOT]
_ (a) that at all times hereafter all freight originating on the lines of the Canadian Northern or on the lines of any of the constituent companies, or on any line or lines of railway now or hereafter owned, leased or operated by the Canadian Northern or by any of the constituent or subsidiary companies, their successors or assigns, shall, when destined to points in Canada, be carried over the lines of the Canadian Northern or of the constituent companies or over some other Canadian railway or railways (which term shall include the line operated by the Canacjian Pacific Railway Company between Montreal and St. John) and that the through rate on export traffic from the point of origin to the point of destination shall not be greater via Canadian ports than it would be via United States ports; and that all inward and outward ocean traffic shall be carried to Canadian ports, and that the Canadian Northern and the several constituent and subsidiary companies shall not in any matter within their power or control directly or indirectly advise or encourage the transportation of any such freight by routes other than those above provided, but shall in all respects in good faith use their utmost endeavours to further the development of trade through Canadian channels and Canadian ports.
At the time this covenant was drafted, in 1914, the Canadian Northern and its subsidiaries were concerns independent of the government, seeking aid for their joint enterprise from the government. In 1918, on the acquisition by the government of the Canadian Northern capital stock, the companies in question were no longer independent of the government, stock control being substituted for covenant control and the policy of the government as implied in the agreement became and has since continued to be the policy of the management so far as Canadian' ports are concerned.

A study of the situation would suggest that farmers would have lost more due to the raising of the minimum weight than they would have gained owing to the corresponding rise in the maximum weight. When the maximum was increased ten pounds the minimum was also raised ten pounds. It is a well known fact that with hogs not bred especially along bacon lines, as was the case with a very large proportion of Canadian hogs, putting them on the market a little on the light side is very certain to give a larger proportion of "selects" than if they were put on the market a little on the heavy side, in which latter case a very large proportion, if not all hogs not especially bred for bacon, would be likely to grade as "thick smooth".

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER AS TO CANADA'S ATTITUDE
speechtext:
In this morning's press I observed an associated press despatch from England referring to a discussion which took place in the British House of Commons yesterday on the second reading of the bill to ratify the Treaty of Peace with Turkey and other instruments that were signed at Lausanne on July 24, 1923. The despatch contains what purports to be certain remarks of the right hon. the Prime Minister of Great Britain with reference to Canada's attitude with respect to the ratification of this treaty. I am unable to say whether or not this report is accurate with respect to the representations it contains.
I have cabled to England to find out exactly what was stated by the Prime Minister. Pending a reply I might quote the reference which appears in the press. The despatch reads:
Canada had replied that she would agree to do what the Imperial government did, Canada had raised one or two constitutional points, which he did not think was really meant by Canada to have much substance but was a sort of safeguard. In order to guard against possible extensions of the principle of the treaty without warning being given Canada desired to retain for herself certain rights of decision over and above the Imperial rights of decision.
I think I should place before the House and the country, in a form which will be immediately available in the Old Land as well, should that be so desired, the exact position of Canada in this matter. Perhaps I can do so most effectively by referring to essential features in their chronological order.
The first communication received by the government with regard to the Lausanne conference was with reference to the invitation which had been extended to different countries to be represented. It was in the nature of a despatch dated October 27, 1922, in which it was intimated that the day before invitations had been sent by the governments of Great Britain, France and Italy to the Japanese, Roumanian, Jugoslav, Greek and Turkish governments, of both Constantinople and Angora, to send representatives to Lausanne on November 13, to conclude treaties to end the war in the East which would replace the Treaty of Sevres;

Treaty with Turkey

that the Russian Soviet government and the Serbian government were also invited to send to Lausanne, at any date to be fixed, representatives to take part in the discussion in reference to the stand which the conference would take at a later stage; that an inquiry was also being addressed by the three governments to the United States, expressing the hope that they would permit the United States representative to be present during the Lausanne negotiations in a capacity similar to that in which the United States representative was present during the negotiations at San Remo in 1920, or to take a more active part in the negotiations, especially on the question of the Straits. According to the arrangements agreed upon with the French and Italian governments, each government was to be represented at Lausanne by two plenipotentiaries. It was intimated that the dominion governments would be kept informed from time to time of the general lines of policy on which the British plenipotentiaries proposed to proceed, and of the course of negotiations; and, in the case of other treaties arising out of the peace, would be invited to sign a new treaty and any separate instrument regulating the status of the Straits. The despatch expressed the hope of His Majesty's government that this procedure would be in accordance with the wishes of the Canadian government.
In reply to the communication I have just referred to the view of the Canadian government was expressed pretty much as follows: It was stated that the government had no exception to take to the course pursued by His Majesty's government with respect to the conclusion of a treaty to end the war in the near East, but that as it was proposed to keep our government informed from time to time of' the general lines of policy upon which the British plenipotentiaries proposed to proceed, and of the course of negotiations, and to invite us to sign a new treaty and any separate instrument regulating the status of the Straits, we deemed it advisable to avail ourselves of the earliest opportunity to inform His Majesty's government that in our opinion the extent to which Canada might be held to be bound by the proceedings of the conference or by the provisions of any treaty or instrument arising out of the same, was necessarily a matter for the parliament of Canada to decide, and that the rights and powers of our parliament in these particulars must not be held to be affected by implication or otherwise in virtue of the information with which our government might be supplied.

That communication was sent on October 31,	1922. We received a little later a
communication from the British government, in which it was intimated that the
British government fully understood that it would be the desire of the Canadian government that any treaty with Turkey, which might result from the conference, should be submitted to the Canadian parliament for approval before His Majesty was advised to ratify it. The despatch further stated that it was the desire of the British government that we should be kept fully informed of the developments of the conference, and that the British government would endeavour to send us full details. That seemed to necessitate making our position more explicit and another despatch was sent to the British government on November 25, 1922. In that despatch it was stated that the Canadian government had not expressed a desire to have any treaty with Turkey, which might result from the conference, submitted to the Canadian parliament for approval before His Majesty was advised to ratify it; nor did we wish to be understood as preferring any such request. We had intended to make it clear that we took no exception to Canada not being invited to be represented at the conference, but that while we had not been invited to participate we had been informed that we should be invited to sign a new treaty and any separate instrument regulating the status of the Straits, we wished to make it perfectly clear that in our opinion the extent to which Canada might be held to be bound by the proceedings of the conference, or by the provisions of any treaty or other instrument arising out of the same, was necessarily a matter for the parliament of Canada to decide. We deemed it of the utmost importance that there should be no misunderstanding as to our position with respect to Canada's obligations in this and kindred matters and we stated that in our opinion parliament would desire, as respected the treaty with Turkey and any other instrument arising out of the Lausanne Conference, to reserve to itself the right to decide, on the merits of the case, what action on the part of the people of Canada was right and proper. In this connection we asked whether we might have authority to place before parliament all the information with which we might be supplied from time to time. The British government intimated in respect to this request that as the conference was likely to be proceeding for some time, it was not desirable that this information should be made public. It was suggested that possibly all that was necessary was that

Treaty with Turkey
parliament should be supplied with a copy of the treaty itself as soon as it was signed.
A further communication was received with respect to our signing of the treaty, saying that the British government had assumed that Canada would wish to follow the precedent set at Versailles and, in accordance with that precedent, authorize some one to sign the treaty on Canada's behalf. The British government having made that representation, we felt it imperative to point out that the procedure which was being followed with respect to Lausanne was not similar to the procedure which had been followed in the case of the Treaty of Versailles or of the subsequent treaty at Washington, inasmuch as both in the case of Versailles and in the case of Washington the Canadian government had been invited to participate in the conference and had been asked to appoint a representative. Such representative had been appointed and duly authorized to represent the country at the conference, and to sign in the name of Canada. We made it clear that the procedure referred to had never been suggested or taken; nor indeed was it possible for us to take it since we had not been invited to participate and that inasmuch as the first stages, upon which the last depended, had been omitted, it was not possible to follow the last stages of procedure adopted at the conferences at Versailles and Washington. Our position in that regard was set forth substantially as follows-I am referring now to the reply to the despatch which intimated that it was expected that we would wish to follow the procedure laid down and adopted at Versailles; we replied that the procedure in respect of the Paris Peace Conference, which was followed, also, later on in connection with the Washington Conference on the Limitation of Armaments, was the procedure to which we understood reference was being made. As to Canada's participation in those conferences we pointed out there were four separate and distinct essential stages, all of importance in the negotiation, signature and ratification of treaties affecting Canada. These stages were, first, the direct representation of Canada at the conferences upon which treaties were drafted, and participation in the proceedings of the conferences by Canada's representatives, each representative holding full powers, signed by His Majesty the King, in the form of letters patent, authorizing him to sign- for and in the name of His Majesty the King in respect of the Dominion of Canada-
-any treaties, conventions or agreements, the Canadian government having by order 60i
in council sanctioned the issuance of these full powers by His Majesty; second, the formal signing of treaties on behalf of Canada by the plenipotentiaries so named; third, the approval by the parliament of Canada of the treaties thus signed on behalf of Canada; and, fourth, the assent of the government of Canada to the final act of ratification, by His Majesty the King, of the treaty signed on behalf of Canada and approved by the parliament of Canada. We pointed out that the British government was quite right in assuming that, as regards the treaties in which Canada was supposed to have a direct or immediate interest, the procedure here outlined was the one which our government would wish to follow, and that in the case of the main political treaties concluded since the war, in general the rule seemed to have been followed that where-ever the dominions had a direct or immediate interest the procedure was shaped to include their participation in the proceedings and their signature of the treaties. That in the case of the conference at Lausanne, the fact that a like procedure had not been followed with respect to representation and participation by Canada had been regarded by us as evidence that, in the opinion of the countries by whom invitations to the conference were extended, Canada could not have been deemed to have that direct and immediate interest which she was supposed to have had in the conferences at Versailles and Washington. In saying this we made it quite clear again that with respect to the course pursued by the Lausanne conference we had no exception to take; with respect to the procedure, however, we pointed out that it must be apparent, quite apart from any action or representations on the part of the government of Canada, that a different procedure had been followed at Lausanne than was followed at Versailles and Washington. Therefore under the circumstances we did not see how we could be expected, in the case of a new treaty or of any separate instrument regarding that treaty,- to follow the procedure adopted in the case of the treaties concluded with Germany, Austria and Bulgaria.
That despatch was sent December 31, 1922. Through the subsequent year we received intermittent accounts of what was taking place at Lausanne, but no further reference to the question of our signature or ratification. This year, shortly before the opening of parliament, we received a communication asking if the Canadian government would concur in the ratification of the treaty which had been signed.

speechtext:
No, nothing
was said further with respect to our position. As I say, we were asked, shortly before the present session of parliament opened, whether the government would signify concurrence in ratification of the treaty and the conventions in question. To this communication we replied: That as Canada had not been invited to send a representative to the Lausanne conference and had not participated in the proceedings there, either directly or indirectly, and for this reason was not a signatory of the treaty, our government did not feel that it was in a position to recommend to parliament the approval of the peace treaty with Turkey and the conventions thereto, and that without the approval of parliament we did not feel that we were warranted in signifying concurrence. Having made our own position thus clear in all its bearings we added, in order that it might not be misunderstood in other ways, that with respect to ratification we would not take exception to such course as His Majesty's government might deem advisable to recommend. We pointed out that our position appeared to be in harmony with the resolution passed at the recent Imperial Conference respecting the negotiation, signature and ratification of treaties, the provisions thereof with reference to signature being as follows:	First concerning such as
impose obligations on one part only:
(a)	Bilateral treaties imposing obligations on one part of the Empire only should be signed by a representative of the government of that part. The full power issued to such representative should indicate the part of the Empire in respect of which the obligations are to be undertaken, and the preamble and text of the treaty should be so worded as to make its scope clear.
As to ratification the concluding paragraph, 2a, reads:
The ratification of treaties imposing obligations on one part of the Empire is effected at the instance of the government of that part:
And secondly, such as impose obligations on more than one part of the Empire:
(b)	Where a bilateral treaty imposes obligations on more than one part of the Empire, the treaty should be' signed by one or more plenipotentiaries on behalf of all the governments concerned.
2 (b) The ratification of treaties imposing obligations on more than one part of the Empire is effected after consultation between the governments of those parts of the Empire concerned. It is for each government to decide whether parliamentary approval or legislation is required before desire for, or concurrence in, ratification is intimated by that government.
We take the position that, not having been invited to the Lausanne conference, not

having been represented there, not having, for the reasons that I have mentioned, signed the treaty, the treaty does not impose obligations on Canada, and that the parts of the Empire on which it does impose obligations are the only parts that should be expected to sign and ratify. As we did not regard the treaty as imposing obligations on Canada, we did not feel that it was necessary to submit the treaty to parliament for its approval, or in its name to signify concurrence in its ratification. A copy of the treaty itself, as hon. members will recall, was laid on the Table on one of the opening days of the session.

speechtext:
Order. We have not
reached the Orders of the Day. It was only by unanimous consent that the Prime Minister was allowed to make his deliverance on a question affecting public policy.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to a point of order. May says that it is not permissible to anticipate the action of parliament or of a com-nfittee appointed by parliament, or to introduce a resolution dealing with a matter already referred to a committee of the House. A few nights ago the House dealt with a proposal with regard to representation and redistribution; therefore I would like to ask if this resolution is in order.

I may say to the hon.
member at once that if the committee were already appointed his obje'ction would perhaps hold. But the committee is not yet appointed, so that I think the resolution is in order.

I do not see what the
committee has to do with it. The matter perhaps not of the whole resolution but of the larger part of it is before parliament now in the form of a bill. The appointment of a committee does not affect the point of order. It might be that the motion could be amended and the part which is not affected by the bill retained, but as it stands it seems to me that the motion is subject to the point of order raised by the hon. member.

The bill to which reference has been made affects the redistribution of the whole Dominion based upon the last census. The proposal in this ease deals with the transferable vote; it deals with the mode of election, not with the redistribution itself. My ruling is that the point of order is not well taken.

I am glad to have permission, Mr. Speaker, to continue, although the hour is late and I proceed in the full knowledge that anybody who wishes to prevent a vote on this question this afternoon may do so by talking until six o'clock.
Last year I had the honour of presenting to the House two resolutions dealing with electoral reform. The first one, having to do with the alternative vote in single member constituencies, was adopted without debate and, I think, with practical unanimity. I am very much pleased to note in the Speech from the Throne that the government will embody this reform in the Dominion Elections Act during the present session. My second proposal was that at the same time
there should be a limited, and more or less experimental, application of proportional representation, which alone would give us a true and adequate representation of the major bodies of existing political opinion. This resolution, after an interesting debate, was defeated by the somewhat narrow majority of eighteen votes. As the Redistribution bill was then before the House and there was reasonable expectation of its being passed before the House prorogued. I took it that the defeat of the motion would postpone any further consideration of the matter of proportional representation until the next redistribution, probably not less than ten years hence. However, as hon. members know'-
I would ask hon. members if they would kindly stop the conversation which is going on in the House, m order that the speaker may have a chance to be heard. I myself can hardly follow his remarks.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. Unfortunately I have a cold to-day and I cannot, speak as distinctly as I ordinarily would.
As I was going on to say, redistribution went over to the present session and I am therefore venturing to ask the House to reconsider the whole question.
The House will remember that the debate which took place last year continued until a very late hour, and owing to the desire of hon. members to reach a vote as quickly as possible I was unable to deal adequately with the objections that had been registered against the resolution. I desire, therefore, to deal very briefly this afternoon with the debate that then took place. I think the whole case against my resolution of last year was pretty well epitomized by the argument of the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen), to which I now propose to address myself.
In opening, my right hon. friend, in his most characteristic fashion, poured ridicule on the government for having no policy in the matter under consideration. Next he embarked upon a rather lengthy digression in order to prove to the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster)-and others-that the great Conservative party was, or at least had been in time past, truly progressive. My right hon. friend's contention in this regard was well sustained by a considerable body of evidence. I have often remarked, as he did on that occasion, that there is nothing so delusive as names. In fact I should not be very much surprised, if we could apply proper standards of measurement, to find Conservatives.
9.50

Proportional Representation
Liberals and Progressives, if these terms have any significance, in all sections of this House. Party names are something like peoples' names: in the dim and distant past they were descriptive, but in process of time they have become mere tags, having no special significance. I presume, Mr. Speaker, that some time in the past my ancestors on the paternal side may have had some admirable characteristics which their descendants have neither the desire nor the right to lay claim to; and I think it is possibly somewhat the same with political parties: whether through marriage, or "morganatic alliance" or the influence of environment, they rapidly change, and the only consolation we have is that it is somewhat easier for them to change their name than it would be for a two hundred and fifty pound Mr. Small to change his name to Mr. Large. However, to digress no further in reply to my right hon. friend's digression, I may say I have no quarrel with his claim that the grand old Conservative party really possesses progressive instincts and has at least some progressive measures to its credit.
Now, coming to proportional representation itself, my right hon. friend seems disposed to endorse the charge so frequently made that this newer method of election will tend toward a continuance and multiplication of groups in parliament, a condition which he believes to be regrettable. He is forced to admit, however, that groups have arisen, continued and multiplied without proportional representation, and he admits further that the emergence and continuance of groups may be useful, holding only that the multiplication of groups does not conduce to the good of the country.
Now, if he could prove that the multiplication of groups was a result of proportional representation, his argument would be valid so far; but he does not prove it; nor can he, for the available evidence points the other way. But, supposing it could be proven that proportional representation resulted in the multiplication of groups, are we justified in concluding that it would be more difficult in that case for the electorate to decide major questions of policy than it has been under the old system? I think not. My right hon. friend's argument in this connection would be valid only if there were a single question of public policy to decide in a general election. In such a case it would not matter very much what sort of electoral methods were in use provided the issue secured a majority vote of the electors. Two parties, one for and the other against, would meet the need. But no general election is IMr. Good.]
like this. There are usually several major issues and a number of minor ones. Then there is the personnel of the administration and its record. Moreover, there are questions pertaining to the qualifications, views anc characters of the various candidates. Proportional representation will give greater freedom of choice to the electors and 4 p.m. thus enable them to give expression to their views on several issues. Nor will it in any way render more difficult the settlement of any major issue, as my right hon. friend seems to think, for will not each candidate declare himself on such issue? Did not the anti-protectionist opinion in Great Britain find expression both in Labour and Liberal candidates, though these may have differed on other questions? And was it not desirable that British electors who wished to record their votes against protection should have the" choice between Labour and Liberal candidates thereby enabling them to register their opinions not only on the major issue but on minor issues as well? I wish to quote, on this point, a paragraph from the last number of the British journal Representation. It is from an article entitled The Three-Party Problem and Proportional Representation :
If public opinion is divided into three main streams, the three party system is not an evil; on the contrary, it is of very great value in the organization of public opinion. The presence of three parties in the general election alone made possible the fairly clear and definite expression of national opinion on the great issues of the day, Protection, Capital Levy, Foreign Policy and Unemployment, and Socialism. Consider what would have happened if the three parties had been reduced to two, Labour and Conservative. The four million Liberal electors would have been compelled to decide whether free trade on the one hand, or the capital levy and socialism on the other, were to them the more important of the issues. Some would have voted for the Conservatives; others for Labour; many might have abstained. Either the Labour party or the Conservative party would have had a majority of seats. In either case, legislation might have been at complete variance with national wishes.
I submit, therefore, Mr. Speaker, that my right hon. friend's argument in this regard, both as respects the connection between groups and proportional representation, and as respects certain effects of groups, is not well-founded.
The next objection put forward by my right hon. friend is the fear that log-rolling may be encouraged by the existence of groups in parliament. Let me read to the House what he says in this connection. I quote from page 410 of Hansard of last year:
The worst thing that can happen parliament is to have it so constituted that policy is determined by a system of exchange of favours, of sectional favours, of favours of any other kind-policy determined thereby rather than determined initially by government on

Proportional
Representation
its responsibility to parliament and ultimately to the electors. For that reason I do not think proportional representation is consonant with the British form of government.
Now, I will agree with my right hon. friend in his objection to log-rolling, but I do not see its connection with proportional representation; in the first place, because we have groups without proportional representation, and in the second place, if proportional representation gave rise to groups, the evils of log-rolling would be no worse than they are under the two-party system, where there are all kinds of opportunities for log-rolling, and that of a secret kind, within the party. How easy it is for representatives to demand local favours as a price of support of a government, how easy for that to go on within a party group if members are so minded. No; that argument is quite beside the mark.
Then finally, after admitting that much may be said in favour of proportional representation, after admitting that such a system tends toward more accurate reflection of all the views of public opinion in the mirror of parliament, my right hon. friend protests vehemently against anything in the nature of a partial or isolated application of proportional representation. Listen to what he says; I am quoting from page 411 of Hansard:
But whether proportional representation is right or wrong, the isolated application of proportional representation is wrong, and wrong in my mind without any room for debate at all. I am against the isolated application of the principle, and would be against it even though the principle itself appealed to me as sound. Now why do I say that? You cannot have the isolated local application of proportional representation while all the rest of the country is under the old system, and either do justice as between party and party or do justice to the constituency to which proportional representation is aplied. It is unfair as between party and party, and it is unfair as respects the constituency itself. Now as between party and party you may apply proportional representation to constituencies, or to classes of constituencies. where one party is the stronger, and thereby deplete its strength in those constituencies but leave unmolested whole areas of the country where another party is the stronger, and thereby give it the whole advantage of its majority over that area. That such a result would be grossly unfair-indeed, that it would be an outrage on the public of this country, there can be no dispute at all, and I do not believe you can choose any area and say that you have chosen this fairly as between the parties represented in parliament.
There are . two charges there; first, that injustice will be done as between party and party, and second, that the constituencies where proportional representation will be applied will not be fairly dealt with. Let us examine these two charges in their reverse order.
Take, for example, the specific case of the city of Winnipeg where proportional representation has been in effect for some years, and to which my right hon. friend refers. In what way has injustice been done to the inhabitants of Winnipeg by providing that the minority in that city should secure representation in the Manitoba legislature? My right hon. friend tries to tell us what injustice is done, or may be done. I shall read a few sentences from his address last year. I quote from page 412 of Hansard:
In a word, the party that directs its policy to winning that vote-
He is referring to the rural vote.
-plays for a stake of forty seats; the party that directs its policy to winning the city vote plays for a stake of one vote or two. As a consequence, there is every motive, there is every political motive-and let us not be so hypocritical as to deny that political motives exercise an influence in parliament-there is every political motive to neglect the constituencies to which proportional representation is applied in the public policy of the country, and to place the whole trend of that public policy in favour of those constituencies to which that system is not applied at all. There would be very little to be gained by any government in office in Manitoba to-day in so turning public policy as to be even fair to the city of Winnipeg.
My right hon. friend is too close a reasoner not to see the weakness of this argument. In fact, he makes a veiled admission when immediately after the sentence I have just read he says:
I do not want to be understood as saying that there has been unfairness to the city.
Well, proportional representation has been in effect in the city for several years. If the menace exists there, why do we not see some realization of it? I think hon. members for that district will bear me out when I say that we have not seen such discrimination against the city of Winnipeg in the Manitoba legislature, and I think for the very good reason that the ten members for Winnipeg elected under proportional representation may be relied upon to protect the interests of the city just as well as any other ten members elected in wards or districts. Indeed, why not? There may be many differences of opinion on other matters of a provincial character, but is there any reason in the world why the ten members elected under proportional representation for the city of Winnipeg, whose opinions may differ on other matters, should not unite in protecting the city against unfair treatment? Why should they not unite to so protect the city?' In fact the members elected in that way would unite to defend the city against any unfair treatment by the province, more

Proportional Representation
so than, ten members elected in wards, because of the fact that ward jealousies and ward needs would probably occupy a somewhat important part in the minds of the members so elected. I think, therefore, Mr. Speaker, that the argument of my right hon. friend with respect to the city of Winnipeg falls down completely.
Nor is he on any better ground when he applies this argument to the federal arena. He says that there are strong sectional interests in Canada. Granted. Why should sectional interests be ignored if members be elected under proportional representation? Does my right hon. friend think that the sectional interests of Nova Scotia would be in greater jeopardy if there were a fair representation of Conservatives from that province in this House? Have not all the members from British Columbia acted unitedly in this House, no matter to what party they belonged, on such a question as that of oriental immigration? Frankly, I see no reason to believe that proportional representation would in any way hinder the united action of representatives from any particular section of the country in regard to sectional needs. On the contrary, it would enable parliament to get a more balanced and accurate view of what the various sections of the country wanted.
Now, so far as justice between party and party is concerned, it is not difficult to see what is in my right hon. friend's mind. He fears, for example, that a Liberal government will apply proportional representation to Toronto and will not apply it to Montreal. Of course injustice may be done in this way, but can it not be done now by the notorious process of gerrymandering? I think, Mr. Speaker, we shall have to depend somewhat on the sense of decency, or at all events on the public protest that would be evoked by any glaring case of that kind. I should like to assure my right hon. friend the leader of the Conservative party and his associates that if they will assist this group in getting a partial application of proportional representation, we on our part will see that they as a party are not unfairly discriminated against.
Now, Mr. Speaker, why do I ask for a partial application of proportional representation? Why do I not seek to apply it all over Canada at the same time? I should like to direct the attention of the House to three fairly definite, and I think fairly valid, reasons for my attitude in that regard.
First, because I am sufficiently cautious and conservative to believe in a not too rapid

change, owing to the ever present danger of reaction. I think we all realize that even progress in the right direction may be too rapid and may bring about a reaction, if the people are not ready for it. "Slow and steady," with the emphasis on the "steady" is, I think, a good motto to keep before us in this connection.
Secondly, because it is generally believed that there are serious practical difficulties in the way of applying proportional representation to very large and sparsely settled areas. Personally, I think these difficulties have been greatly magnified, but it would be folly to ignore such belief as exists in this connection. It seems to me to be the part of wisdom, therefore, to await the result of experience. Most people are profoundly affected by actual experience, and by keeping this in mind I think we shall make greater progress in the long run than if we were to go too fast at the start.
Thirdly and finally, because while the task of the voter under proportional representation is easy, the task of the returning officer is not so easy, and in order that there may be a minimum of mistakes in the actual carrying out of the count in the various constituencies, it is desirable, in fact it is absolutely necessary, that there should be at least one trained supervisor, and it woulc be better to have several, in each constituency where such an experiment is tried We have some men in Canada who are prepared to supervise the count, but we have not very many, and it would give the system a black eye if, by attempting to apply it where people are not prepared to intelligently supervise the procedure, we should fail down in the application. In that way the system would be veiy unfairly judged.
For these reasons it seems to me desirable to make haste slowly. What objection would there be, for instance, to the application of proportional representation in Winnipeg for federal purposes, where they have already had it for provincial elections for a number of years? I cannot see any difficulty about applying it in such a case. People are familiar with the procedure. There are plenty of skilled returning officers in Winnipeg to look after the count. But the situation might be very different, indeed, if we were to make the attempt in one of the large and sparsely settled areas of northern Ontario. I think that what we ought to do would be to adopt it where it is immediately practicable and extend it as fast as it is shown to be wise.
Now, Mr. Speaker, leaving the debate of last year, let me submit to the House some

Proportional Representation
information which experience has given us during the intervening period. First of all, in point of interest, I think, are the Irish elections of last summer. In this connection I would like to quote from the October number of the Proportional Representation Review. This is from an article on the Irish Free State elections and I quote as follows:
The election of the Dail Eireann (Chamber of Deputies) of the Irish Free State, was carried out on August 27, by proportional representation with the single non-transferable vote (the Hare system). The 153 members were elected from 30 districts returning from 3 to 9 members in each. Generally speaking, each county was a district. The city of Dublin, which returned 15 members, was polled as two districts. The result may be summarized as follows:
Then there is a table showing the name of the party, the number of votes polled, the seats obtained and the seats in proportion to votes. I do not think it is necessary for me to weary the House by reading the whole of this table. There were five different parties or groups who appealed to the electors of Ireland last summer: The Government party, Anti-Treaty or Republican party, Labour, including Independent Labour, Farmers, Business and Independents. Further down in this article, I should like to quote the following comment:
A system of election which thus gives even-handed justice to every party, even one whose leaders are in jail or "on the run," may be thought by some to be too liberal for the safety of the state. But that is not the view of those Irishmen and others who seem to us the true heirs of the great tradition of Anglo-Saxon statesmanship exemplified by such men as Pitt and Burke and Lincoln. For Americans especially it should not be hard to appreciate the profound advantage of a system of election which gives justice in representation. If the British parliament had supported Burke on March 22, 1775, when he advocated the recognition by parliament of "the ancient constitutional policy of this kingdom with regard to representation" and its application to the rebellious Americans, it would doubtless have held the colonies. The system of election used in the Free State, by giving justice (so far, we mean, as the system is concerned) even to those in rebellion against the existing government, has tended to discourage unparliamentary methods.
There is another paragraph which I shall not read, dealing with the steadying influence of proportional representation. The change of representation from that of the previous parliament has not been very noticeable, and therefore greater harmony and continuity have been possible. I should like to note in this connection also some information given in the British .journal, Representation, to which I have alluded before. This is from an article on the Free State elections of 1923:
A method of election is something more than machinery. It influences profoundly both the character of the electoral campaign and the nature of its result.
And further on:
The influence of proportional representation can be traced even in the nominations. Apart from Dublin University, which was permitted to return unchallenged three Independents, every constituency was contested. Further, the four parties-Government, Republican, Farmer ,and Labour-had their standard-bearers, not merely in reasonably favourable constituencies, but in practically all. This did not, however, necessitate any extraordinary number of candidates.
I would like to comment at this stage that the charge which has been frequently made that this method of election results in a multiplicity of candidates as well as a multiplicity of groups, is utterly without foundation in actual experience. I continue:
There were for the 150 contested seats in Ireland, 373 candidates.
Then it gives the statistics for Great Britain in the election of 1922 and the election of 1923, showing that under the proportional representation system, the proportion of candidates running was practically no greater than under the system which prevailed in Great Britain.
I have in my hand a letter which appeared in the London Times not long ago from Lord Monteagle, commenting upon the Irish election. After an introduction, he enumerates as follows certain broad characteristics of the Irish election of last August:
(1) The peaceable and orderly character, not only of the polling day, but of the preliminary campaign, was as generally recognized as it was unexpected. The surprise indeed was natural when one remembers the passion and lawlessness of the previous twelve months then hardly allayed, and recalls the election disturbances of former days even in ordinarily peaceful times. The charge may surely be attributed largely to the decrease of the gladiatorial element inherent in single combat contests.
I shall not weary the House with reading the rest of this enumeration, which is very interesting, indeed, showing the unusually useful and harmonizing and stabilizing effects of this method of election in Ireland. Surely, if there is any place where the utility of this method of election had a better chance to be proven to the hilt than Ireland, I would like to know where it is.
I refer next, just for a moment or two, to the British elections of last December. On the whole, a much fairer representation was secured than in the British elections of the previous year. 1922; but this was purely by accident. That that is so, can be definitely proven by an analysis of some of the constituency or borough and county elections. I quote from the British journal, Representation, for February, 1924, a little information bearing upon this point. For instance, in the city of Birmingham, the Conservative party, with 149,000 votes, secured eleven representatives. The Liberal party, with 76,000 votes, secured none

Proportional Representation
at all. The Labour party, with 28,000 votes, secured none at all. There you have about two-fifths of the votes securing the total representation in the city of Birmingham. In Cornwall, the Liberal party captured all of the seats, while the Conservative party, with 41,000 votes, secured no representation at all. If you take Wales and Monmouth together, you find that the Labour party secured a great preponderance of the representation. In Scotland also the Labour party secured a preponderance of the representation. Therefore, as I said, it is only by accident that the result on the whole comes out with a greater degree of fairness than we would expect. The situation is simply this, that Conservatives in Scotland and in certain other sections have to be content with being represented by Conservatives from cities such as Birmingham, just as in this parliament the Conservatives of Nova Scotia have to be content to be represented by the Conservatives of Ontario. I might make the same comment with respect to other provinces of the Dominion.
I should like also to refer in passing to a very interesting election which took place last November under this system in the city of Cleveland, the fifth city in importance and population in the United States. The city was divided into four districts and twenty-five couneilmen were elected in it. I have here in the January number of the Proportional Representation Review a very exhaustive account of this election. I will not weary the House by making any quotations from it, although I should like to do so, if I had the time. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that anybody who reads this careful analysis of the actual experience of Cleveland must come to the conclusion that the method in this instance has a great many most important advantages.
Now let me refer to an interesting news item from New Zealand, which is, I think, of particular interest at this time:
In New Zealand an electoral development of importance has taken place, a bill having been introduced by the government involving a partial application of P.R. in the House of Representatives. The new bill proposes P.R. for the chief cities, Auckland with 5 members, Wellington, 5, Christchurch 4 and Dunedin 4, -in all 18 members in a House of 80. Preferential voting (the alternative vote) is to be applied in the remaining constituencies. The government introduced the bill, with a view to making its provisions generally known, immediately before the parliamentary adjournment last August, and the Prime Minister stated that he "intended, all being well to proceed with it next session." As both the opposition parties, Labour and Liberal, are pledged to P.R. there is hope that a definite advance will be made.
The situation in New Zealand apparently is almost identical with the situation in this country, save that the government here has

not yet adopted the policy of making an experimental application of proportional representation to certain selected constituencies.
I must refer also to the Ontario elections of last June, when the Conservative party, with a minority of the total vote, secured a very large majority of the representation. Hon. members are aware of the effort made by the preceding administration to	enact two
measures of electoral reform and redistribution just prior to the dissolution of the legislature last summer, and we are all familiar with the methods which were used to block those reforms and with their final failure. As a result of the failure to introduce better electoral methods in Ontario last June, we find that the Conservative party, with 49 per cent, of the vote, secured 66 per cent, of the seats; the Farmers, with 22 per cent of the vote, secured 16 per cent of the seats; the Liberal party, with 21 per cent of the votes secured 12 per cent of the seats; while the Labour and Independent vote of 7 per cent secured 5.8 per cent of the representation. Although the Conservative party may regard this situation as being very satisfactory, it is something which will undoubtedly prove a boomerang. No party which secures more than a fair share of representation ought to hold it or can hold it very long. As I remarked last year when the matter was under discussion, the farmers in the preceding government in Ontario had more than their fair share of representation, and perhaps it was that fact w'hich to some extent led to their defeat on June 25.
In Manitoba also we find that recently the legislature has adopted the alternative or transferable vote for single-member constituencies, and there is a movement on foot to extend proportional representation outside the city of Winnipeg. I notice that two clippings, one from the Tribune and one from the Free Press, which I have here, refer to a resolution brought in by Mr. Tanner, the member for Kildonan and St. Andrews, who is apparently moving for an extension of proportional representation to some of the more thickly settled districts outside the city of Winnipeg. I merely refer to this in passing as indicating the tendency of the times. I should refer also to the situation in Alberta where, I understand, it is proposed at the next session of the legislature to adopt the alternative vote and proportional reprensenta-tion for the whole of the province'. It is too soon, perhaps, to speak definitely as to what will be done, but I understand that this is the prospect. And I notice that even in Quebec there is a considerable sentiment in

Proportional Representation
favour of reform along these lines. Perhaps the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) will be particularly interested in an article from the Quebec Chronicle. The first paragraph reads:
Although the adoption of the proportional representation system of election makes comparatively slow progress in this country, the time is declared to be coming when the sheer force of example will break down all opposition. In this connection, no doubt, the statement will come as a surprise to many readers that well over one-eighth of the earth's population, it is stated, are living in proportional representation territory; that is nations or other governmental units throughout which proportional elections are held for important representative bodies by direct popular vote.
The rest of the article contains a lengthy enumeration of various countries in which this system is in use.
Now, why should we not be satisfied with the alternative vote? Last year apparently there was a feeling that if we secured one reform we should be satisfied with that. But the alternative vote, I would point out, is designed to meet a special difficulty which has been arising in recent years, the difficulty namely, in connection with the running of more than two candidates in a single-member constituency. The alternative vote meets that difficulty satisfactorily. Every one recognizes that, and that is why this House has adopted it without debate and, I think, with practical unanimity. But it does not secure or assure to us fair representation. It cannot do so, and we must go further as quickly and yet as carefully as we can. In the little magazine to which I have already referred there is an analysis of the last British general election from the point of view of the alternative vote. This article, which is very interesting, shows that, so far as can be ascertained from an analysis of that election the alternative vote would not have been of very great value in securing a fair representation in Great Britain. I do not want the House to think that I am minimising the importance of the alternative vote at all; it is very important, and I am glad that we have attained it. But nevertheless it does not meet the problem which democracies have to face at the present time. I will not impose upon the House the details of this analysis of the British elections from that point of view, but they are worth looking into.
Let me refer for a moment to the language of the resolution. Hon. members will see that it is somewhat different from the resolution of last year which was defeated by the small majority of 18. It occurred to me that possibly, as that resolution apparently was not acceptable to the House, there being no evident desire to adopt proportional representation in certain selected constituencies, the House might at least agree to apply proportional representation in any multimember constituencies that might remain after the next redistribution. In the past we have had several two-member constituencies, three of which I recall at the moment,-Halifax, St. John and Ottawa. There may be others.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There are five-Cape
Breton South and Richmond, St. John. Halifax, Ottawa, and Queen's, Prince Edward Island.

I am glad to have that information. If the House cannot see its way clear now to go to the length which I suggested last session, and if these two-member constituencies are retained and possibly other multimember constituencies are brought into existence in the proposed redistribution, I think we might as well utilize the transferable vote in such constituencies to secure a fairer representation. Let me illustrate what I mean by taking the case of the city of Halifax. Let us suppose that 55 per cent of the electorate would vote Conservative and 45 per cent Liberal. Obviously it would be much fairer to have one Conservative and one Liberal representing that city in this House than it would be to have two Conservative members returned, as would almost inevitably happen under the present system even with the alternative vote. A two-member constituency is not the best for the application of proportional representation, but it is better than nothing.
If the House will not go so far-and I think it was a very moderate length to which I asked it to go last session-then perhaps it would be agreeable to adopt what I am now suggesting in this resolution. I should, however, be most happy if a member of the government, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) for instance, could see his way clear to bring in an amendment in accordance with the terms of my resolution of last session, not specifying any particular constituencies, but leaving it in the hands of the committee on redistribution to consider whether or not Winnipeg, for example, might not be selected as a federal constituency in which to apply this method. But, as I have already said, I chose this particular wording, feeling that it was the least the House could be asked to adopt, and in the hope that something might be done in this direction. I gather from the remarks made last year by the present Solicitor General (Mr. McMurray) that he is not sympathetic to proportional representation being applied to Winnipeg, but I am disposed rather to accept as of more weight the very many assurances

Proportional Representation
from other prominent men in that city that the system is satisfactory there.
Personally I think we might at least go this far, and I am simply submitting it to the House as a matter of opinion. We might at least apply the method in the present two-member constituencies, if they are continued, or in any inultimembered constituencies. I think we could apply it in Winnipeg without any disturbance of local conditions. I should also like to see it applied in Toronto and Montreal. And I should be glad to see an experimental test made in old Ontario where we have a fairly dense mixed rural and urban population. I do not see any difficulty in its application to such a territory. As I remarked on a previous occasion, the committee of the Ontario legislature which had this matter under study some two or three years ago recommended two experimental applications of the system in mixed constituencies, one in western Ontario and one in eastern Ontario. I know that in my own district we might group together the counties of Brant and Oxford, and possibly Norfolk, to the south, forming a group-constituency which would elect about five members.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would submit to the House and to the government that now is the only chance we shall have within the next ten years to make any headway with this most important reform, a reform which has shown itself by actual experience to be an improvement on our present system. I do not want to be arbitrary, neither do I want to ask too much, and I should be most pleased if the government could see its way to consider some further application of proportional representation than I have suggested in this resolution; and, I repeat, I would welcome an amendment to that end. But, if no hon. member cares to bring in such an amendment, then I must be content with this resolution, which simply asks the House to endorse the very minimum application of the principle that is possible in Canada at the present time.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the hon.
member (Mr. Good) deserves credit for the consideration he has given to the improvement of our system of representation, more particularly as concerns proportional representation-a system which is in force in many countries of the world, and which will probably be in force later on, at least partially, in this country.

The resolution, however, suggests that the Dominion Elections Act be amended so as to use the transferable vote to secure as far as possible proportional representation in such multimembered constituencies as may be constituted by the next redistribution. In other words, he asks the House to legislate for a condition which may or may not exist after the redistribution committee has completed its work and the bill has become law. In this respect at least the resolution is premature. Personally, I would rather see some of our double-member constituencies wiped out. As I said a few minutes ago, we have five double-member constituencies at the present time-Ottawa, Halifax, St. John City and Counties of St. John and Albert, Cape Breton South and Richmond, and Queen's, P.E.I. By his resolution my hon. friend would ask the House to apply proportional representation to such constituencies as these. I do not think it would be giving a fair chance to the system of proportional representation to try it in those constituencies instead of in the big cities as the hon. member suggested last year. I myself voted for the resolution he introduced last year, but it was voted down by the House.

La majorite n'avait
pas raison.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

My hon. friend says the House was wrong; perhaps that is so, but I could.not help it. I think that if a trial is to be given to proportional representation it ought to be in such cities as Toronto-I believe Toronto would be the best one-Montreal, Winnipeg and Vancouver, but not in Queen's, Prince Edward Island, for instance, which is largely a rural constituency, or in St. John City and Counties of St. John and Albert, or in Halifax, which also are largely rural. As I said a moment ago, I do not think proportional representation would be given a fair trial in counties where it could not best demonstrate its advantages.
I do not like the suggestion of trying out proportional representation in a sort of makeshift way instead of discussing it and applying it openly on its merits. If proportional representation is to be introduced in Canada it should enter by the front door instead of by that sort of back entrance. I really think it is not the best way to try the system. Last year the House accepted the principle of the transferable vote, and in a very short time the government will introduce a bill to give effect to the unanimous resolution adopted at that time.
