speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Well, I am very sorry
indeed that my hon. friends did not register their protest in a more striking way, because the resolution was declared carried without anybody speaking against it, so far as I can remember, and then we proceeded to discuss the following resolution, which dealt with proportional representation. My hon. friend probably intends to oppose the change which will be effected by the bill to be introduced by the government. However, I think we stand a fair chance of getting the legislation through parliament.
I think my hon. friend (Mr. Good) should be content with this measure of progress, for which he is largely responsible on account of the consideration he has given to the question, the amount of work he has done in that connection and the remarks with which he accompanied his resolution of last year. My hon. friend himself has said that we should move slowly, that we should not progress too rapidty. Festina lente-make haste slowly-was an old axiom of the Romans, and I believe that in any movement of this kind we must not go too fast, otherwise we may run into danger. I think my hon. friend might well await the report of the committee on Redistribution before pressing his motion.

Mr. Speaker, I am in the same
position as the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) in regard to the statement made by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe): I remember distinctly that when the motion on the transferable vote was put last year practically all those in this quarter of the House said "no". It is quite true that a division was not demanded. I think myself that that was a mistake. In conversation with a great many members on the other side of the House I have ascertained that if .a division had been demanded on that occasion they
would have voted against the resolution. I do not believe that the resolution by any means represented the unanimous opinion of this House, and I do not believe that if the matter came before the House again, except as a government measure, any unanimous vote in favour of the transferable vote would be recorded. I believe, on the contrary, that if the supporters of the government could vote on the question as an independent measure they would vote against it. Of course I realize that if it comes before the House as a government measure the supporters of the government will feel compelled to vote in favour of it.
Did the resolution come before the House last year as a government measure?

I am not suggesting
that. That is what I was trying to make clear; it came up just as it came up today, without the members generally knowing it was coming up and without their being properly prepared to speak on it. How many places in this chamber are vacant on this occasion? How many hon. members are not present? We must all be interested in this question, because it is a very important one, and I suggest that if some method could be arrived at whereby all hon. members irrespective of the party affiliations should have the privilege of voting on the question again-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If my hon. friend will allow me, does he not know that a few minutes after this motion was adopted last year, another motion, that declaring in favour of the principle of proportional representation, was defeated, the vote standing 90 to 72, which shows a considerable attendance of the members?
That does not show the attendance of the members when this particular question was being discussed. As a matter of fact the House will'probably fill up a little later when a division comes on today.
Is my hon. friend not aware that the adoption of this resolution last year without division took place almost immediately after three o'clock in a very full House?
My statement is this: That that resolution was passed last year without proper consideration, and I back up my assertion by statements made to me by many hon. members on the other side.

Name them.

Proportional Representation

I am not going to name them; it would take me too long. As far as I am concerned I am absolutely opposed even to the transferable vote feature of this resolution, and I always have been. I think that every member of the official opposition is also opposed to. it. Moreover, the resolution suggests that we should make an experimental test of proportional representation in an actual election. Now I would warn the House against anything of that kind. We have been making experiments with proportional representation in British Columbia for some time. We have tried it out in most of our cities. We have tried it out in Victoria, Vancouver, New Westminster, Nelson and other municipalities, and so far as I am aware, not one of these municipalities that experimented with the system follows it today. They decided that it was not a proper system.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
You mean proportional
representation?

Yes, and the single
transferable vote. Both have been discarded, as the experiments proved the system to be unsatisfactory. The results speak for themselves. I might say that before this system was adopted by the cities in British Columbia it was discussed at length, and its advocates addressed public meetings and elaborated their arguments in detail. They had a Proportional Representation society out there, with branches in all the cities. So the people did not jump into this thing with their eyes shut. They tried the experiment after carefully considering the arguments pro and con, and they expected to see the results the advocates of this system had claimed for it. But they were disappointed; in actual practice it did not prove a success. And, if that was the case with us in British Columbia, why should we suppose that we shall be any more fortunate when we apply it in Dominion elections? As far as I am concerned I am absolutely opposed to these experimental tests. I do not believe in this system at all. I would rather let somebody else do the experimenting, and then when we have seen some system that works well in practice, one that is no longer in the experimental stage, we can adopt it. I am absolutely opposed to the spirit of this resolution.
Why?

So as to make my
position perfectly clear I say without any hesitation that I am opposed to the principle of proportional representation. I am also

opposed to that abbreviated portion of it known as the single transferable vote. I would suggest in all sincerity that this House consider very seriously before attempting to adopt the suggestion contained in 'this resolution.

The Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) referred a moment ago to the unanimous adoption of this resolution last year. I took occasion to interrupt him, and say that so far as I was concerned I voted "No" when this resolution was called. The question has arisen why this resolution was allowed to pass last year without discussion. I recall the occasion very well. Personally I have given a great deal of thought and study to this problem for a number of years, and I have never been able to bring myself to an approval of this system of voting.
When this question was called
5 p.m. last year I waited both for a presentation by the hon. member introducing it, who I believe spoke very few words, as Hansard will show-

May I ask the hon. member
if he does not recollect the full discussion of the matter that was presented the previous year? Last year I said very little about it, simply to save time.

Quite true, the hon.
member discussed it the year before; I am not questioning his good faith in the matter for a moment; he has been quite sincere and has given this subject a great deal of thought and study; I am simply stating what occurred last year. My hon. friend introduced his resolution with a very few words, and I awaited some utterance by the government in regard to the matter, but not a word was said. One hesitates always to rise to his feet and be the first, as it were, to oppose these things, and I certainly hesitated. The resolution passed, with very great regrets afterwards for having let the motion pass. Immediately the second resolution was called dealing with proportional representation, the two having been divided on that occasion, I rose to my feet and opposed it very vigorously, and later that motion was voted down. I want to say to the House that a great many members came to me afterwards and expressed regret that the first motion had carried without discussion. I merely refer to that in justice to myself with reference to the interruption I made a moment ago when the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) was speaking. While the records show the motion

Proportional Representation
was carried without division, I regret that there was not a full discussion and a division on this very important subject.
I purpose giving to the House a few reasons why I am opposed to this resolution. I agree with the hon. member to my left who asked the previous speaker (Mr. McQuarrie) why he was opposed to this system of voting, that we should state our reasons why we are opposed or favourable, as the case may be. I have not come this afternoon prepared with any careful analysis of the problem. I am speaking largely from memory and from what thought I have given to the subject previously, and if my arguments are a little disjointed it is simply because I have not had the time this session to prepare any orderly address on the subject.
My hon. friend who introduced this motion intimated in his argument that this system is designed to give different groups in the community representation in the House. Indeed, this is one of the main arguments, one of the chief supporting pillars of this so-called electoral reform-that it does give representation to a variety of groups of interests in the country. On the other hand, it is also argued that parties need not have any fear of it because parties are preserved under it. Now I submit that you cannot have both; you cannot change the present system into a group system, and at the same time preserve the party system. I am not for the moment arguing pro or con. I am merely replying to the argument which is very frequently presented as one of the main reasons for the introduction of this reform. As a matter of fact, I think the tendency of the system is to multiply groups. It does not follow as a logical conclusion-it does not follow as night follows day-that that would be the result, but the general tendency is to increase the number of groups in a legislature or parliament. I want to seriously direct the attention of the House, and particularly the attention of the government, to the consideration of this particular point. I feel that perhaps this is the crux of the whole business; therefore let us ask ourselves the question, is it desirable to change or to exchange the present British parliamentary system now in vogue in Canada for a group system similar to that in vogue in France, in Switzerland, in Belgium and in many other European countries? That is the question which I propound, and that is the- question to which we should give consideration.
Let me examine the proposition for a minute. The genius of the British parliamentary system is that an individual elected to parliament is elected as a representative of all the people; that is that he is not elected to represent the peculiar interests of Vancouver Centre or Winnipeg or Montreal, Toronto or any other section. He or she is elected to represent the interests of all the people of Canada in any matter that comes before parliament. As far as human nature will permit, that individual is supposed to examine each measure in the light of the interests of the country at large. I quite frankly agree that very often we will, selfishly perhaps and in varying degrees, place local interests before national interests. But, heavens, we are not infallible creatures? We are all fallible, all liable to err and do err, but that does not condemn the system or the principle underlying it. We are elected to represent all the people of the country, and the further we get away from that principle, and the more parochial our representation in this House becomes, the less efficient, the less noble is the institution of parliament. If we depart from that principle through error or fault, that is corrected by the electorate at each election if they so choose. But if we are going to depart from it deliberately by changing that system for a new system, let us examine the new system and see if it is a great improvement over the other, or if it is any improvement at all. My hon. friend (Mr. Good) made a point which is frequently made, and I have heard others make it and advance it as an unanswerable argument. I will take my hon. friend's illustration. He says that it is not right that the Conservatives of Nova Scotia should have only one representative in this House when they polled a certain number of votes in the last general election. He inferred that proportional representation or the single transferable vote, to the extent it was used, would correct this evil. Would it correct the evil? That is the question before us. I will admit if it corrects the evil-if there is an evil- then there is something in his argument. But does it infallibly correct it? Take Australia, where proportional representation is carried out in all its glory-

May I interrupt the hon.
member to say that proportional representation is not in existence in Australia.

I notice some of my
hon. friends are very prone to applaud the minute anybody makes a positive statement. My hon. friend will admit that proportional representation is in force, in so far as the elections to the Senate are concerned. Am I right or wrong?

As respects the Senate, yes.

Proportional Representation

Now will my hon. friends applaud me? I was about to say that this system in all its glory was tried out in Australia in connection with the Senate. In the elections of 1919 there were cast 860,000 Liberal votes, which elected 17 members to the Senate, and 820,000 Labour votes which elected one member. There were cast 173,000 Farmer votes which elected no senator. In other words, under proportional representation, which is supposed to be an infallible cure for the so-called evil of minority control, the situation is that with 860,000 votes the Liberals had 17 seats in the Senate, while with 993,000 votes the Labour and Farmers parties had only one seat between them in the Senate. I am not saying anything against the principle, because of that; but what I do say is that the imaginary evil, if I may use that term, of minority control, or of a group that has not a complete majority of the votes, having control of the government is not such a terrific evil after all; and furthermore that it is not corrected by the proposition now before the House.

Could the hon. gentleman
give us more information as to the details of the votes, the number of groups and the number of constituencies?

I did not come into the
House with all the information I might have had. I am giving my hon. friend the facts. As I go along I will try and adduce certain facts which I think will support my argument fairly well. I have not the information my hon. friend asks for.
Turning to another matter, it was intimated by the hon. member who spoke a short time ago (Mr. Good) that consideration should be given to this as an experiment, that we ought to try it, and I think the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) suggested that we should try it in Montreal, Toronto, Winnipeg and Vancouver. Let me say that we tried this system in the city of Vancouver for three full years. We had three different elections with proportional representation and the transferable vote. The mayor was elected under the single transferable vote, and the alderman, eight of them, were elected under a system of proportional representation in all its ramifications and perplexities.

What was the system
of proportional representation under which they elected the city council in Vancouver? Was it the Hare system and the single transferable vote?
They had single transferable vote for the mayor and the eight alderman were elected under the proportional representation system.

There are a number
of systems of proportional representation. The best known and most widely used is the Hare system, the single transferable vote for the multi-member constituency. Was that the system?

I cannot tell you the
exact breed of it, but when it came to a plebiscite of the people, it ran like a hare, so that I presume it was the Hare system. I am sorry I cannot give my hon. friend the exact brand. It was proportional representation in all its ramifications. Probably this fact will enlighten my hon. friend. It took at least two weeks to count the ballots, so that I presume it was a real proportional representation system. Furthermore they had to bring in trained experts and accountants to count the ballots. That would be added evidence that it was the real proportional representation. It was tried for three years. The first year there was a fairly large vote, probably- the same as usual. In the second year the vote dropped to 6,000 out of some 42,000 on the list, and in the third year, only 10,000 votes were polled out of 44,000 on the list. The reason was that people lost interest in the system for the election of representatives. Last summer, independently of an election altogether, the city council submitted to the electorate a plebiscite. I have in my hands a facsimile of the plebiscite, in fact, one of the ballots sent to me by the city clerk, together with his letter. This ballot is headed:
City of Vancouver. Municipal Proportional Representation Act.
Then the question is asked:
Are you in favour of rescinding the adoption of the Municipal Proportional Representation Act in this municipality? Yes No.
Underneath the following instructions are given to the voters:
If in favour of rescinding the adoption of the Municipal Proportional Representation Act, place a cross thus (X) opposite the word "yes". If against rescinding place a cross (X) opposite the word "no".
That is a plain, simple ballot, and a plain question to the electorate whether they are in favour of retaining this system or of rejecting it. I have in my hand a letter from William McQueen, city clerk of Vancouver, in reply to an inquiry by me as regards this plebiscite. The letter is dated March 13, 1924, city clerk's
961,

office, Vancouver, B.C. It is addressed to myself and it reads:

I read that for this reason: In our city, after a deliberate trial of this system for three successive years and on a plebiscite submitted to the people, this system was rejected by a vote of more than two to one. I submit to my hon. friend that it would not be reasonable or fair to impose upon the city of Vancouver at least, a proportional representation system when the people of that city have so clearly expressed their view in opposition thereto.
What is the total vote in Vancouver?

I quite foresee what my hon. friend desires to know. I told him a moment ago that the number of voters on the list the year before was 44,000, and I told him also that under proportional representation the total vote polled at an annual election had dropped down to 6,000 because of the complexity of the vote, plus this-and I am in a position to give you only my word on this, but I know it, because I have studied the question and obtained the views of electors as far as possible-that the electorate became convinced that they could not secure a proper interpretation of their wishes at the polls under proportional representation. I know that is exactly contrary to the claims made for this system, but as a matter of experience that is the case. I* venture to say that if hon. gentlemen will inquire carefully amongst the electorate where this system is in vogue, they will find that a substantial majority of the people amongst whom they inquire, if they inquire impartially, hold exactly that view, that this system does not do what it is supposed to do or what is claimed for it by its leading advocates, that is, give a frank and clear expression to public opinion.
Further, in regard to the query of the hon. member for Brant, I know that he will compare the vote polled with the 44,000. Let me defend my position in regard to that, and in order that we may have the matter on Hansard correctly, let me add this vote up. The total vote polled was 5,514. There was no election; but let me say to my hon. friend this, that there has been in existence in Vancouver, for at least ten years, a virile, active organization, advocating the adoption of this system of voting, a Proportional Representation Society, with regular officers, holding meetings constantly during the last ten years, advocating this system, annually attending the counting of the ballots, analysing the system, advertising its good features and so forth. So, when the test came, when this plebiscite was submitted, this association was behind the system, whereas those opposed to it were not organized at all; theirs was simply an expression of opinion of whoever chose to go to the polls. Therefore, the small number of votes polled on the plebiscite should not be quoted as wiping out, as it were, the significance of the majority in the case.
Let me turn to another phase of this question. It is claimed for proportional representation and the single transferable vote that it eliminates the chance choice; that is, supposing you have three candidates and one is elected with less than a majority of the votes, that is an unfair representation of public 'opinion. It is claimed in behalf of this system that it is scientifically, mathematically correct. Am I stating the claim unfairly? I think my hon. friend will agree with me that that is claimed for it. My hon. friend shakes his head. He is the first supporter of it who has ever admitted that it is not supposed to be mathematically correct. I am glad he does admit that, because it shows his fairness and honesty. It is not mathematically correct. It has in it the element of chance, the same as the other method. Let me try to explain this. I am not in a position to demonstrate it with figures. One would need a blackboard and to have the thing worked out by way of small fractions to do so, but I think I can make the matter clear to the House, perhaps in a somewhat rambling manner. This is a case that occurred in Vancouver in one of the elections. I think there were about 28 candidates for eight aldermanic positions. I cannot give the exact figures of the vote and the division of them; it would be interesting if I could; but I will give just the outline. The system followed was this: When the city clerk had ascertained what the quota for election would be-in this case



Proportional Representation
it was about 800 or something of that kind- then as regards such individuals as received jver the quota of 800, the excess of their votes over that quota was taken, then the second choices were counted and distributed amongst the other candidates. I ask the House: Upon what basis of science, if you like, upon what basis of equity did they take that particular man? Why should they take his counts any more than the fourth, fifth or tenth man's counts? The choice is an arbitrary one. You choose arbitrarily; you might just as fairly have chosen the fourth or the fifth man as the first man.
Or let us turn the thing around the other way. Assume for a moment that none were elected on the first choice, which often is the case; because you frequently have a long list of candidates. What is the arbitrary rule followed in that event? It is to take the lowest man and to tell him, "You go, you are finished." Why do you take the lowest man? Just on the same principle exactly as the lowest man is told now that he is defeated. In other words, there is no more justice, no more science, no more logic in it, not one particle, than there is in the present system, and it is just as arbitrary. What are the circumstances? Two men might join their forces for the purpose of trying to secure the election of one of them; and in the case I have in mind neither of the candidates who ran in that way was elected until the seventeenth count. On the seventeenth count one of them, was last, the other being just above him. It was the last man's turn, under this arbitrary method, to be discarded and his seconds chosen. His seconds were chosen, and the two of them having run together, as it were, neck and neck, they naturally at that particular moment elected a man who was lowest on the list over another person who had led him all through the count to that moment.. There is nothing particularly fair about that. As a matter of fact, the man who was ahead of him in all equity was entitled to election rather than the man who was second below him. I want therefore to impress upon the House the fact that this system is not equitable but is just as arbitrary as the present method of electing representatives, with the one difference that the choice is divided up into an indefinite number of different selections according to the number of candidates on the list.
After all, what is the test of all systems of government-what is the real test? Can we not find it in the periods of history of any country under any given system of government? You do not test any system of gov-I Mr. Stevens.]
ernment by some mathematical scheme of counting ballots; that is not the way to test the efficiency or the justice or the fairness of government. The system of proportional representation has been in vogue in different countries for some time now and is practised in France, in Belgium, in Switzerland, in Portugal and elsewhere on the continent of Europe. On the other hand, the system that has been followed in Great Britain, in Canada and in other parts of the Empire for so long a time is the present method of electing members to represent the people in the various legislative bodies. I agree for the moment, for the sake of argument, that this method has developed the party system, but I do not wish to digress in order to discuss that point. At all events, we have in Canada the representative system of government which has had such excellent results in Great Britain and throughout the Empire, and under which individuals aie selected to represent all the people in parliament, to study and determine upon the affairs of the country at large. Will anyone suggest that the countries of Europe outside of Great Britain-France, Belgium, Portugal, Switzerland, Norway, Sweden-have been better governed than Great Britain? Will anyone suggest that any of these countries, during the last fifty or hundred years has stood out before the world as giving a better expression of government than has the British Empire?
I contend that not one of them has. And what better test of the efficiency of any system of government can there be than that? What has occurred in France? Again I must apologize for not having the exact data, but hon. gentlemen, I am sure, will accept my word for it that the system of proportional representation was adopted in France some years ago.
It is not the same system.
My hon. friend is a trifle too exact; it is one of the systems.
And not a very proper one.

There are no two countries that have precisely the same'form of this system, and that is the peculiarity of it. Some one suggests that it is like Heinz'3 pickles, having 57 varieties; yes, and as an hon. member observes, it gets you into the same pickle. After all, the proportional representation system is the same-I was going to say principle-but lack of principle-wherever it is in force. In France they have the same system in a different form from that

Proportional Representation
which is followed in Switzerland and Belgium, and as a result of the practice there they have seven or eight different groups; so that, as an examination of the facts will show, during the last twenty or twenty-five years France has had a change in government - on an average every year. In fact, that has been the case for the last fifty years.
My hon. friend will admit that a change of government in France does not involve the same consequences as it does in Great Britain.

I frankly admit that it is a different matter altogether. But the change in government in France is made simply by means of a compromise between groups; and although M. Poincare the other day was defeated on a technical vote in the French House of Deputies he simply fished around, after his resignation, and got together out of the various groups another government to carry on. And in this morning's papers it is stated that this new government, in office only a few days, is faced with an angry wave in the Chamber of Deputies because of something that does not suit some of the groups. The point which must be clear to all is that none of these countries has had the same stable government which has obtained in Great Britain; and a comparison of the general results obtained under the old system in Great Britain and under the new system in these other places must, I think, show quite clearly that the British government stands out above all others in so far as stability, strength and world influence are concerned. Before we bring about any change in principle in our system of electing members of parliament, I think hon. gentlemen would do well very seriously to consider the results under the two systems, by comparison over a period of years. If such a comparison is made I am convinced that it * will show that the British parliamentary svstem is superior to the other. If that is the case, as I submit it is, then we ought to proceed with great caution in any attempt to abandon that principle for the adoption of an entirely new one.
Let me turn to another phase of the question. I shall perhaps be treading on slightly dangerous ground, but I desire to touch upon this point notwithstanding. We hear a great deal in these days about democracy. I made a few observations on this subject recently outside the House, and perhaps hon. members will pardon me if I introduce some of the arguments which I then advanced. Personally I have always had a very strong tendency towards what might be called democratic
61i
methods, using the term " democratic " in a broad, general way. But when we are dealing with a proposal for an entire change in our principles of government, I submit we ought to pause and carefully analyze our present system. It is in fact made up of three elements. It is not a pure democracy at all. We have a limited monarchy, represented in the King; we have autocracy, represented in the House of Lords and the Senate; we have pure democracy, represented in the House of Commons. I am quite aware that there are those who favour wiping out the first two elements altogether. But I say to every thoughtful member of the House, we ought to study with extreme care the advantages or disadvantages, as the case may be, of the presence of those two elements before we suggest discarding them. The more I study the history of the British parliamentary system of government, the more I am convinced that the kingly power, in the person of the King in Great Britain and of the Governor General in Canada, and the autocratic power, in the House of Lords and the Senate respectively in these two countries, serve a very excellent purpose in our system of government.
Let us take, for instance, the kingly power. Mr. Speaker, I am quite aware of the rule that we should not in our debates refer to the King, but I am speaking solely of the elements of government and shall keep within the rules of the House. At one time the kingly power was regarded as an individual and absolute right. That is not the case today. As a matter of fact, the Governor General here, or the King in Great Britain, is the last court of appeal of people who might consider themselves suffering some abuse at the hands either of the House of Commons or of the Senate or the House of Lords respectively. And British history records that during the past century or more the Crown has exercised its prerogative far oftener in the interests of minorities whose liberties were being encroached upon than arbitrarily for the benefit of the ruling classes. Therefore I appeal to the House to most carefully examine the workings of our present system before we attempt to change it in any way.
Let me take another step in this analysis. In connection with proportional representation there goes another departure from our present system. I venture to say that if this resolution passes and its provisions are embodied in the law, my hon. friend who has introduced it (Mr. Good) will be prepared to present to the House at some future session -if he is still a member-a resolution in

Proportional Representation
favour of the initiative, referendum and recall. This innovation has a certain attraction for those who have a penchant for proportional representation. In other words, the two go together. But it is equally doubtful whether this other reform has any advantages to recommend it more than the reform now suggested. After all, public opinion is not infallible. I know there are those appealing to the public who like to declare that the people s opinion is infallible. Indeed, anyone uttering my views is in danger of being bianded an autocrat. But let us consider the matter coolly and frankly. How can every individual in the nation be, as a unit, fully apprised of the complexities of certain questions that come before parliament? It is an utter impossibility. No bill can be drafted so clearly as to convey of it full effects to the public. Yet under this new system, which I say is correlated with the subject matter of the resolution, an appeal is made to the public and the decision is to be left entirely with them.
I think I have discussed the resolution at sufficient length. I only regret that I have not had the time to present to the House a more detailed analysis of proportional representation supported by figures and other evidence. I will conclude with an appeal to the House to give the very fullest consideration to this principle before they adopt it as a definite change in our electoral svstem.

Now let me consider some of the arguments used by my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens). He said that that interesting city had tried this scheme for the long period of three years, and had then found that it was inadvisable to continue it on a plebiscite in which about four thousand of [DOT] the people voted out of forty-four thousand, and the system was abandoned by a considerable majority. I hold in my hand a clipping from u paper entitled, The Joke on Vancouver. It reads as follows:
The city of Vancouver, after using proportional representation for two or three years in its municipal elections, discarded it and went back to the old system this year. The' argument used against proportional representation in Vancouver was that it had made no difference in the election results. Scores of citizens were quite sure that the same men would have been elected under the old system as under proportional representation; therefore, why introduce a more complicated system when it gave no benefit? One of the men who was most active in the fight to discard proportional representation was L. D. Taylor. In the election a few days ago Mr. Taylor was one of the mayorality candidates in a three-cornered contest. The other candidates were Alderman Owen and Alderman Pettipiece. Owen was elected. Pettipiece was the low candidate. It is now realized at Vancouver that if proportional representation had been in force Taylor, in all probability, would have been elected when Pettipiece would have been counted out and his votes distributed. Discussing the situation, the Vancouver Province says: ' " ' Poetic justice,' is how Mr. Garfield King, one of the principal proponents of the proportional representation system in the city, describes the result of the mayoralty election.
" Under proportiona! representation, he believes that Mr.	D. Taylor would have received a larve
majority of the 2,459 votes polled for Alderman Pettipiece.
So it would appear that perhaps the system which was tried out in this city might be a good system, even though it was abandoned for the time being. Winnipeg has

Proportional Representation
had this system for a number of years; it has operated in several elections and has given satisfactory results there. It would appear that the counting of the votes caused great objections to the system as applied in Vancouver; whether the. people of Winnipeg were better mathematicians than those of Vancouver is a question which I will not attempt to answer. What we want in this country is representative government. Do we get representative government under our present system? We do not get thoroughly representative government under a system which will allow great political parties to remain unrepresented in this House when the number of their adherents in the different provinces runs into some thousands. The hon. member for Vancouver Centre has made an appeal to British practice and to British tradition, and he is quite right in that. I will draw his attention to the words of a great British statesman, the Hon. Herbert H. Asquith, who, in advocating proportional representation, said, "There should not be a strain of public opinion unrepresented in this House."	'
The tendency may be, it is stated, to multiply groups. I doubt that, but if there are substantial groups of public opinion in this country unrepresented by the official parties it is infinitely better that those groups should be multiplied in order that every strain of public opinion may find expression in this House. I cannot believe that parliamentary institutions will be effective unless proper provision is made for different strains of public opinion. It may be that in the future we will be unable to divide the Canadian people into two great groups. It may happen that we may have that system restored, and it may be that another system may have to be worked out. I believe that this system of proportional representation offers a reasonable and proper method under which sincere differences of public opinion may be represented. There is a great deal of artificiality in the present condition of our political parties and the present division. Why, we had the other day the member for West Toronto (Mr. Hocken) urging the old Liberal principle of representation by population, and we have the member for Vancouver Centre to-day talking very much the way a Stuart talked at the time of Cromwell. The appeal to British tradition was somewhat strange in view of the fact that we have to-day a group system of parliamentary government in Great Britain. We have a Labour party on the treasury benches, and it represents a minority of the people and a minority in the House.
Government by minority.

"Government by minority," ejaculates the member for West Toronto. It is quite true that in the future the minority whose views correspond more nearly than the views of any other group in the House may be given the responsibility of government with the control exercised by other groups in the House. That is a possible development of our British constitutional system. Our British constitutional system is not remaining the same; its very flexibility is one of its greatest virtues.
Now, I approach the discussion of this question this afternoon in very much the same position as the member for Vancouver Centre:
I had not expected to take part in the debate and I have not material under my hand for a discussion of the matter in detail. But the point to be remembered is this: That our present system does not accurately or adequately reflect the differences of public opinion in our country and we have to seek out a method other than the method at present adopted. I think the sparseness of our population in most parts of this country makes proportional representation impracticable. In our large areas in the western provinces, in rural Quebec and in rural Ontario, I do not believe that in most cases proportional representation is possible, but I do believe it should be adopted in the large cities. I believe it should be adopted in Toronto; I believe it should be adopted in Montreal.
It would not make any difference in Toronto.

I do not know whether it would or not, but it would do this: If there are ten seats in Toronto and there are twenty or thirty per cent of Liberal votes in Toronto, then out of the ten seats the Liberals would get two or three. And the same way in Montreal: if there is a small proportion of Conservatives in Montreal this system would give them proper representation. To-day we find that Toronto is represented entirely by Conservatives and that Montreal is represented entirely by Liberals.
No-Liberals in name, some of them.

At least they are counted as Liberals, and for the purposes of my discussion I will do them the compliment of calling them Liberals. I say that it is an unwholesome condition-and anyone who thinks for a moment will agree with me-to have the representation of one great city all one way and the representation of another

Proportional Representation
great city all the other wtay, especially when the number of people belonging to the different political parties make that representation an untrue and improper representation of the public opinion of those cities. What we want in this country is a method of election which will ensure an adequate and proper representation of the real thoughts and the real opinion of the people upon public matters.

Mr. Speaker, I am afraid that the three minutes left before six o'clock will scarcely be long enough to give the explanation I should like to make in reply to the question asked by the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster). I was not aware that this resolution would be debated to-day. I have listened with a good deal of interest to some of the statements which have been made, and particularly to the references that have been made to a resolution calling for the transferable or alternative vote which was passed at the last session of parliament. A good many things have happened during the past year; a good deal of light has been thrown on the actions and motives of some of the people of this Dominion as well as of other countries, and I think it is about time that we were speaking frankly what we believe to be the fact, and that we should cast aside this camouflage which has been attempted by a good many people of this Dominion so far as political parties are concerned.
To my mind the object that is sought by the alternative vote, which is coupled with this resolution, is one that is intended to *arry out the designs of the members of the .wo parties calling themselves the Progressive party and the Liberal party, whereas, as a matter of fact, there is absolutely no difference between the two. I think the people of this country thoroughly understand their object, what they have in view, and the means by which they are going to take advantage in a scheme of this kind. For that reason I must say that I am absolutely opposed to any further experiments along the line suggested by the most impractical members of the House, the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Good), and his colleague the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster). They are always ready to venture into some field where no definite results are in evidence; yes to enact freak legislation, as one hon. member suggests.

prominent men in connection with matters which are affected by the resolution before us. With your permission, Mr. Speaker, I should like to refer to the remarks that were made by one or two speakers on that occasion. I quote from the Ottawa Journal of March a year ago:
Mr. J. W. Curry, K.C., M.L.A., Toronto Southeast, seat " A," after saying that the convention of eastern Ontario Liberals was to him an eye-opener, proclaimed himself a consistent believer in Liberalism which meant progress and the betterment of the people.
